doc.title: John Abercrombie interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Jimi Hendrix and rock guitarists
summary: Hendrix was the one rock guitarist he truly listened to, leading him to a fuzz tone and wah-wah; he never saw him.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I consider Hendrix was like, he was the one rock & roll guitarist that I really listened to. I mean I didn’t really listen to a lot of the other guys. I mean I heard them, I liked some things, but when I heard him it was like listening to a jazz musician but playing a different kind of music. He played so fluid and liquid and just soulful and he was so creative that he could have been playing anything. It could have been any instrument. The vocabulary was not jazz like I know jazz, but it felt really improvised. It felt loose too. It felt like it really had a loose kind of jazz quality. I just think he was just, he was the one I mean I kind of got when I heard that, when I heard an album called “Axis Bold as Love” that’s when I went and bought a fuzz tone and a wah-wah pedal. And I said I really like this stuff. I want to, I don’t know if I want to play like that but I mean I wanted to try to do some of that you know. And that was I think he had that impact on a lot of jazz musicians and not all the rock musicians did. You know I mean but Hendrix I think universally probably had a strong impact not only on guitar players but on a lot of people that grew up in my period, horn players, everybody, it was like, they’d hear it on a record and they’d know immediately it’s Jimi Hendrix. The other guys I couldn’t tell particularly. Later in years I wound up really liking Eric Clapton, but I didn’t really care for Cream all that much. I mean I thought it was very interesting but it was kind of like a wall of notes that never really — it had a lot of energy to it and excitement but I didn’t
really get the melody to it. It didn’t seem very melodic. And I thought Hendrix was very melodic.

No I never did. I’m surprised I never did because I saw so many great jazz musicians and I was in that scene playing with fusion bands but I never got to see a lot of the great rock players. I played opposite Chicago once, I remember that, and that was really enjoyable and I heard some bands, that band Mountain one time with Leslie West, it was so loud my stomach was rumbling. I had to leave. It sounded good but I remember it was in the Village Gate and it was just like the music had me pinned against the wall.
